title: Wound healing and abnormal scars: keloid or hypertrophic?

guidelineVersions: International clinical recommendations on scar management (Mustoe et al., 2002; updated Gold et al., 2014)

brief.scenario: Miss Tamsin Oduya, 24, had an epidermoid cyst excised from her right shoulder 8 months ago. The scar is now raised, red and itchy and has spread beyond the incision. She is unhappy with it.
brief.task: The examiner will read out written findings of the scar and then of its histology. Answer questions on wound healing, abnormal scars and their management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Four overlapping phases; abnormal scars come from a prolonged inflammatory and proliferative response.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Offering excision alone for a keloid.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "A scar spreading beyond the original wound is a keloid."

grid.label: Phases of healing
grid.fail: Omits haemostasis or remodelling, or gives the phases out of order.
grid.pass: Haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, remodelling: overlapping, not sequential steps.
grid.high: Timing: inflammation in the first days; granulation from about day 4; remodelling from 2 to 3 weeks for a year or more.

grid.label: Cells and collagen
grid.fail: Cannot name the cell that lays down collagen.
grid.pass: Neutrophils then macrophages; fibroblasts lay down type III collagen, replaced by cross-linked type I in remodelling.
grid.high: Macrophages drive the switch to repair; myofibroblasts contract the wound; the scar never regains the strength of normal skin.

grid.label: Keloid or hypertrophic from the findings
grid.fail: Calls a scar extending beyond the wound hypertrophic.
grid.pass: Keloid: grows beyond the original wound and does not regress. Hypertrophic: stays within it and may improve with time.
grid.high: Adds risk factors: shoulder, anterior chest and earlobe sites, darker skin, family history, adolescence, wound tension.

grid.label: Histology
grid.pass: Keloid: thick, hyalinised, eosinophilic 'keloidal' collagen bundles, sparse in hypertrophic scars.
grid.high: Explains both as chronic inflammation of the reticular dermis, driven by tension, with many blood vessels in keloids.

grid.label: Treatment
grid.pass: Silicone gel sheeting and intralesional corticosteroid (triamcinolone) first; pressure therapy.
grid.high: Excision alone has a high recurrence rate, so only with adjuvant steroid or radiotherapy, and a low-tension closure.

grid.label: Counselling
grid.pass: Realistic expectations: flatter and less itchy, not gone. Warns of steroid atrophy, hypopigmentation and telangiectasia.
grid.high: Advises avoiding elective procedures or piercings in keloid-prone skin; would biopsy an atypical or ulcerating scar.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd explain it should become flatter and less itchy but won't disappear. Steroid can cause thinning, pale skin and small vessels.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How long does each phase last?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Inflammation in the first days, granulation tissue from about day 4, and remodelling from 2 to 3 weeks for a year or more.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Macrophages drive the switch to repair, myofibroblasts contract the wound, and the scar never regains the strength of normal skin.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why did she get a keloid?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The shoulder is a high-tension site, and she's young. Darker skin and a family history also increase the risk.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Both scars are chronic inflammation of the reticular dermis, driven by tension. Keloids have more hyalinised collagen and more vessels.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Excision alone has a high recurrence rate. If we excise, it's with a low-tension closure and adjuvant steroid or radiotherapy.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: She should avoid elective procedures or piercings in keloid-prone skin. If it ulcerated or changed, I'd biopsy it.

failures.move: Excising a keloid without adjuvant treatment.
failures.consequence: High recurrence, often larger than the original.
Wrong counselling: she is told it will settle when it will not.
Cannot confirm the diagnosis on histology.
Cannot explain why scars change for months.

recovery.line: The key question is whether it has grown beyond the original wound.

knowledge.fact: Remodelling starts at 2 to 3 weeks and lasts a year or more.
Keloid: beyond the wound margin. Hypertrophic: within it.
Keloidal collagen (thick, hyalinised bundles) is the histological marker of keloid.
Silicone gel sheeting and intralesional corticosteroid have the best evidence.
Combination treatment is advised; the 2014 update favours more aggressive early keloid treatment.

recall.think: Recurrence after surgery; missing a malignancy in an atypical scar.

numbers.meaning: remodelling begins, lasting a year or more

recall.trap: A raised red scar is not always hypertrophic.
recall.finish: Steroid and silicone; excision only with adjuvant treatment.

partner.opening: Before I read out the findings of her scar: what are the phases of wound healing?

reveals.finding: Read out: on the right shoulder there is a firm, raised, shiny, red-purple scar about 4 cm by 2 cm. The original incision can be traced as a 2 cm line within it, and the raised tissue extends well beyond that line into the surrounding normal skin, with claw-like projections at its edges. The surface is smooth and the skin over it is intact.

Read out: the H&E section of a biopsy from the scar shows the dermis largely replaced by thick, glassy, brightly pink-staining bundles of collagen lying haphazardly among finer collagen fibres, with scattered fibroblasts and small blood vessels. The overlying epidermis is thin and intact.
Her brother has keloids on his chest. The scar itches at night.

push.question: Which collagen is laid down first, and what replaces it?
push.expect: Type III, replaced by cross-linked type I.

push.question: Is this keloid or hypertrophic? Why?
What would you offer first?
push.expect: Silicone gel sheeting and intralesional triamcinolone.

push.question: She wants it cut out. What do you say?
push.expect: High recurrence alone; only with adjuvant steroid or radiotherapy.

curveballs.prompt: Why use radiotherapy for a benign condition?
curveballs.safeAnswer: As an adjuvant after excision of resistant keloids, to reduce recurrence, after discussing its risks.

curveballs.prompt: A long-standing burn scar has ulcerated.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Biopsy it to exclude squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin's ulcer).

curveballs.prompt: Where on the body are keloids least likely?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Sites with little skin tension, such as the upper eyelid, scalp and anterior lower leg.
